# Continual-ARC task-f94f8cc4: boundary rails, marker rays, and color-4 markers

## When to Use
A mostly uniform field contains equal-length colored rail segments on opposite boundaries and sparse signal cells of another color. Signal cells become color 4; matching-color rays connect each signal to its aligned rail, while signal offsets along that rail are projected onto the opposite rail as full-length perpendicular rays. Preserve both rails. Use this rule when the two rails and signal offsets match the demonstrated setup; if a fresh grid breaks those structural conditions, request a demo rather than indiscriminately filling rail rows.

## Demonstrated facts
- Geometry is preserved.
- Original boundary-rail cells stay unchanged.
- Signal marker cells become color 4.
- In marker rows, the marker-colored fill extends along the row toward the applicable boundary rail, stopping before/at the rail and preserving the rail color. Exact direction depends on the arrangement.
- Some rail-aligned rows without an input signal also receive fill. The selector for these extra rows is unresolved; do not indiscriminately fill every row or the full rail span.

### Demo 1 (6x5)
Background 1; boundary color 2: left edge at rows 1–2 and right edge at rows 4–5. Signal color 5 at `(1,2),(2,2)` (0-based). Output changes the signal cells to 4, paints `(1,1),(2,1)` color 5, and paints columns 0–3 of rows 4–5 color 5; boundary cells `(4,4),(5,4)` remain 2. Other cells stay unchanged.

### Demo 2 (9x18)
Background 2; boundary color 8: right edge rows 0–2 and left edge rows 6–8. Signal color 7 at `(7,13),(8,13)`. Output paints rows 1–2, columns 0–16, color 7 (right boundary remains 8). On rows 7–8 it paints columns 1–12 color 7, changes each signal at column 13 to 4, and leaves columns 14–17 at background 2. Row 0 and row 6 remain otherwise unchanged.

### Demo 3 (26x23)
Background 8; boundary color 6: left edge rows 0–9 and right edge rows 15–24. Signal color 7 occurs at `(15,18),(16,3),(17,5),(18,6),(19,16),(20,17),(22,20),(23,8)`. Every listed signal becomes 4; in each such row, cells strictly to its right through column 21 become 7, with boundary color 6 retained at column 22. In addition, rows 0–5 and 7–8 are filled color 7 in columns 1–22, while rows 6 and 9 remain background 8 beyond the boundary cell. This extra top-left rail-associated fill is an important exception to the simple ray rule; do not infer a general selector from this one case alone.

## Solved test evidence
22x6, background 9, boundary color 1 at right edge rows 5–10 and left edge rows 16–21; signal color 8 at `(5,2)`. Correct output:
- Change `(5,2)` to 4.
- Paint `(5,3),(5,4)` color 8, stopping before the boundary cell `(5,5)=1`.
- Also paint `(16,1)..(16,5)` color 8; preserve `(16,0)=1`.
- Leave all other cells unchanged.
This extra fill on row 16 was essential: a candidate that painted only the marker-row ray was wrong. Do not assume that the test's extra-fill relation (row 16 opposite row 5) explains the more complex demo extras; it is an observed test fact pending a complete rule.

## Practical procedure
1. Identify uniform background, boundary rails, and signal color; record rail spans and signal coordinates.
2. For this task variant, two rails may be equal-length segments on opposite boundaries. Color each signal 4 and extend its signal color from the rail inward through the signal's row, stopping at the signal (the signal is replaced by 4).
3. Project each signal's offset within its rail segment onto the opposite rail's segment. For each projected row, fill a perpendicular ray through the interior, preserving the opposite boundary rail. Confirm orientation and projection against demos; do not fill all rail rows.
4. Replay the transformation on each demo: Demo 1 uses a top-left rail (columns 0–6, rows 0) and bottom rail (columns 14–20, row 17), with color-5 signals at (9,14),(13,15),(13,16),(14,20),(15,18); outputs recolor signals to 4, paint leftward rays on the signal rows to the left of each signal, and project each signal's row offset from the top rail onto the bottom rail as vertical rays upward. Demo 2 uses a top-left rail (row 0, cols 0–2) and bottom rail (row 21, cols 5–7), color-8 signals at (13,7),(17,5),(19,6); outputs recolor signals to 4, paint leftward horizontal rays to the top rail's x-range, and project the signal rows' offsets onto bottom-rail rows 13,17,19 as vertical rays up to row 1. Existing rail cells remain unchanged.
5. Validate dimensions and preserve every cell not licensed by the learned rule.

## Recovery note
Two earlier guesses on the solved test were incorrect: (a) filling broadly across both boundary rails and (b) filling a whole lower-edge band. Another guess omitted the extra row-16 fill and was also incorrect. The confirmed test output is the exact delta listed above; an incorrect-only score does not identify which component of an extrapolated rule failed.

## Additional solved test evidence (5x17)
A fresh test had background 9, color-6 boundary rails at row 0 columns 0–7 and row 4 columns 9–16, and color-1 signals at `(2,2),(2,3),(2,4),(2,7),(3,0),(3,1),(3,6)` (0-based). The confirmed output preserves dimensions and both rails, changes every signal to 4, and adds color 1 at exactly these background cells:
- Row 0: columns 9–13 and 15–16.
- Row 1: columns 0–4, 6–7, 9–13, and 15–16.
- Row 2: columns 0–1, 5–6, 9–13, and 15–16.
- Row 3: columns 9–13 and 15–16.
Everything else remains as input. The exact submitted output was correct. This is independent evidence that target-color rays can form segmented bands on both sides of the grid, with gaps retained; do not simplify the output to only direct marker-row extensions. The extra-fill selector remains incompletely characterized, so preserve this as an exact precedent rather than generalizing beyond the rail/marker geometry.

## Additional solved test evidence (6x24)
Background 2; color-1 boundary rails at top row columns 0–6 and bottom row columns 13–19. Color-0 markers at `(2,18)` and `(3,14)` (0-based). The confirmed output preserves both rails and changes the markers to 4. It adds color 0 as two vertical rays: column 5, rows 1–5, and column 1, rows 1–5. All other cells remain unchanged. The marker columns project across the lower rail segment to the top rail segment by relative offset: column 18 is offset 5 from lower rail start 13, mapping to top column 5; column 14 is offset 1, mapping to top column 1. This provides a concrete horizontal-rail orientation precedent: marker offsets select columns for full interior vertical rays, while original boundary rails are preserved.

## Additional demonstrated evidence (two more demos)

These exact deltas strengthen the model that a sparse marker selects a ray toward the nearer/opposite boundary rail, and its relative offset in one equal-length rail segment is projected onto the paired rail. Signal cells turn into 4; fill uses the signal's original color; rail cells remain unchanged.

- **16x21 demo:** background 7; color-2 vertical rails at right edge column 20, rows 0–4, and left edge column 0, rows 11–15. A color-1 marker at `(0,1)` becomes 4. Row 0 columns 2–19 become 1 (column 0 remains 7 and column 20 remains 2); row 11 columns 1–20 become 1 (column 0 remains 2). All other cells stay unchanged. Thus the marker row's ray points toward its right rail, while the corresponding offset row on the opposite rail receives an inward ray.
- **10x24 demo:** background 7; color-8 rails at left edge column 0, rows 0–1, and right edge column 23, rows 8–9. A color-0 marker at `(8,4)` becomes 4; row 8 columns 5–22 become 0, preserving the right rail. Its offset 0 within the right rail projects to row 0 of the left rail: row 0 columns 1–23 become 0, preserving `(0,0)=8`. All other cells remain unchanged.

## Additional solved test evidence (28x24, task-f94f8cc4)

A fresh test was solved with the established vertical-rail rule. Background 7; color-5 rails at right edge column 23, rows 2–8, and left edge column 0, rows 21–27 (equal length 7). Color-3 signal cells at `(2,11),(3,4),(5,9),(7,14),(8,6)` (0-based). Correct output preserves both rails; changes all five signal cells to 4; and fills color 3 strictly to the right of each signal through column 22 in its signal row. It also projects each signal row's offset within the right rail segment onto the left rail: rows 2,3,5,7,8 map respectively to rows 21,22,24,26,27, where columns 1–23 are filled color 3 and the left boundary rail remains 5. Unselected projected rows 23 and 25 remain unchanged. All other cells are preserved. This provides a clean solved precedent for the vertical-side rail configuration and confirms exact offset projection plus rightward marker rays.

## Failed test instance caution (25x16; eight wrong submissions)

Input: background 5; color-2 boundary segments at top row columns 3–8 and bottom row columns 10–15; color-6 sparse markers at (6,7), (15,8), and (21,5),(21,6). Eight candidates failed. All attempted marker recolors to 4 and/or marker-color rays/vertical projections based on segment offsets were wrong, as were variants filling column bands. No correct output is known. This instance is strong evidence not to extrapolate the straightforward rail/marker projection model merely because there are two boundary segments and sparse markers: their positions/geometry did not satisfy a sufficiently validated condition. The demos received included a 24x17 case with top-left short rail (row 0, cols 0–6) and bottom rail (row 23, cols 7–13), color-0 markers at (10,12),(15,10),(20,13). Output drew vertical color-0 rays on columns 3 and 5–6 over rows 1–22, and column 12 rows 11–22; marker cells changed to 4. Another 6x29 demo had boundary rails at row 0 cols 16–24 and row 5 cols 0–8, markers color 7 at (2,20),(2,21),(2,24),(3,19). Output filled color 7 leftwards from each marker to col 3 in marker rows, but changed markers to 4 only at (2,21),(2,24),(3,19); marker (2,20) stayed 7 because it was incorporated into the fill. In the 24x29 demo, rails are vertical side segments: color-7 rails at left col 0 rows 7–11 and right col 28 rows 19–23; color-6 markers at (7,14),(9,21),(10,22),(11,10). Fill color 6 runs across rows 7,9,10,11 from the left rail toward each marker (but not past marker), while markers become 4; the right rail projects color-6 full horizontal bands onto rows 19,21,22,23 except the rail column, while row 20 stays unchanged. Thus shape/orientation differ across demos, and projection/fill directions depend on a more nuanced selector. Request demos or derive stronger rule before trying similar unexplained structures. Do not reuse failed candidates from this case.

## Failed test instance caution (14x18)

Input had background 8, color-2 horizontal rails at the top-right `(row 0, columns 16–17)` and bottom-left `(row 13, columns 5–6)`, plus color-5 markers at `(2,6)` and `(6,5)`. Eight submissions were incorrect. In particular, the simple guess that the two marker cells become 4 and the right-edge columns 16–17 are filled color 5 through most/all interior rows was wrong, as was a guess adding downward rays from the markers while retaining those full right-edge bars. These are counterexamples to projecting markers indiscriminately to the opposite edge or treating the rightmost rail as the target for all markers. This test's correct output is unknown; do not record any candidate output as solved. On future related inputs, use a discriminating demo when horizontal rails and marker alignment do not directly instantiate a verified precedent, and reason carefully about which rail contains/aligns with each signal and how offset projection selects the opposite rail cells.

---
name: arc-grid-reasoning
description: Use for ARC-style grid puzzles. Infer rules from examples.
---

# ARC grid reasoning

Use this skill for ARC and ARC-like grid tasks, including continual streams where each instance is independent and the response protocol is strict.

## Core workflow

1. **Read the task protocol first.** Record allowed actions, attempt/demo caps, and exact output format. For a stream protocol that requires one action JSON on the last line, emit exactly one action per turn; do not add explanation or unrelated tool output to the answer.
2. **Inventory the grid.** Note dimensions, background color, non-background colors, connected components, repeated shapes, symmetry, and isolated markers. Distinguish the likely source object/template from the objects that indicate where or how to apply it.
3. **Extract rules from every demonstration.** Compare input and output cell-by-cell. Track what stays fixed, what changes, what is removed, and what is added. Test whether changes are local to markers, aligned to object bounds, or global. Prefer a compact rule that explains all examples, not just one visually salient feature.
4. **Resolve anchor and orientation explicitly.** For any copied or expanded pattern, determine whether the marker denotes the top-left, center, endpoint, or another anchor. Check rotations/reflections, direction, offsets, boundary clipping, and overlap behavior against demonstrations. Do not assume a component is copied around every marker merely because its shape looks like a template.
5. **Use demos strategically.** Request another example only when there is a concrete unresolved distinction between plausible rules and the expected information could change the answer. After receiving one, analyze it before requesting another. Avoid repeated requests made without extracting the information already supplied; each request has a cost.
6. **Construct and validate the candidate.** Preserve dimensions unless examples establish otherwise. Build the result systematically, then check every modified cell against the inferred rule, preserve all unaffected cells, verify row widths/heights and palette, and inspect overlaps and edges. For generated grids, prefer a small script or explicit coordinate transforms over manual copying, then inspect the complete serialized grid.
7. **Submit only when the rule is adequately supported.** If there is a correctness response, use it to update the hypothesis rather than repeating the same transformation. A wrong submission is evidence that some assumption—often anchor, direction, overwrite semantics, or which object is the template—was wrong.

## Aligned-panel nonzero overlap (validated task-04691f01)
When a full uniform row or column separates two equally sized aligned panels, produce a single panel with color 2 exactly at coordinates where both corresponding input cells are nonzero; output 0 everywhere else. The task has a persistent 10x15 vertical-divider variant: a full color-8 column at c=7 leaves 10x7 panels, with a sparse color-6 marker field on the left and sparse color-4 markers on the right (background 0). Output is 10x7 with 2 iff both aligned panel cells are nonzero. This recurrence's accepted output had exactly three 2s at output coordinates (r,c)=(4,5),(5,6),(7,6), all other cells 0. Another task-04691f01 demo had a full color-9 horizontal divider: the upper 7x27 panel was mostly 8 with sparse 0s, and the lower panel contained 0s and sparse 7s. The 7x27 output had 2 exactly where upper!=0 AND lower!=0 (equivalently, upper=8 and lower=7 in that demo). In the test, a full color-6 divider separated 3x27 panels, the upper panel was mostly 1 with sparse 0s and the lower mostly 9 with sparse 0s; the correct result was 2 where upper=1 AND lower=9, and 0 otherwise. The lower panel's nonzero field color may vary; do not assume a particular palette or rely on dominant-color matching without checking the nonzero-overlap rule. Preserve aligned coordinates and discard the divider and source panels. This rule is also consistent with other aligned-panel marker/field examples; verify the exact predicate from each demo.

## Repeated stencil in a noisy grid

Some tasks use a small colored seed object as a stencil: find every translated location where each seed-colored footprint cell falls on the grid's designated target color, then recolor those footprint cells with the seed color. **Do not assume the target is the most common/background-looking color**: infer it from demonstrations by testing exact matches of the seed's occupied footprint against each plausible color and comparing the resulting changes cell-by-cell. In a demonstrated case, the target was color 0 even though the noisy field's dominant color was 3 (and another demo's dominant field color was 8); matching the majority color produced many false placements, while exact color-0 matches explained every output change. Check only the seed's occupied cells: holes in its bounding box may contain arbitrary noise and do not constrain a match. The rest of the grid—including other noise/background-looking colors—stays unchanged. Infer the stencil from the seed's color cells within its bounding box, preserving holes and disconnected cells; do not fill its full rectangle unless the seed occupies it. Validate by checking every occupied footprint cell at each candidate, then union placements (overlaps are harmless when they use the same color). This pattern is demonstrated by examples with random noise and sparse, non-rectangular seeds. A confirmed variant uses a 3×3 color-5 seed with occupied offsets {(0,2),(1,1),(1,2),(2,0),(2,2)}; color-4 noise fills much of the grid, but valid translated stencil locations are exactly those where all five occupied offsets are color 0. Overlay color 5 on those five cells, preserve the other cells (including the stencil's holes), and allow matches to overlap.

## Line-directed object translation with a trailing highlight

A recurring pattern is a full straight line in one color and a separate compact object elsewhere, both oriented so the object can move toward the line along the perpendicular axis. Demonstrations may show the object translated until it is directly adjacent to the line, with a strip in a third color (observed color 8) placed immediately on the object's far side, opposite the line. The strip matches the object's cross-section: a 1×N object produces a 1×N strip, while an M×N rectangle may produce an M×1 strip. Verify which object moves, that the full line remains unchanged, the direction and adjacency, and the exact trail location/width from demos before applying. Preserve the object's shape and colors. For a test case, move the smaller separated object toward the complete line until it touches, then place the demonstrated highlight strip just beyond it on the away-from-line side; leave all else unchanged.

## Hypothesis discipline

- Maintain a short list of candidate rules and the observation each predicts. Eliminate candidates using exact coordinates from all demos.
- Separate *what* is transformed (markers, components, rows/columns, background regions) from *how* it is transformed (copy, recolor, extend, tile, rotate, connect).
- Avoid anchoring on one example or a familiar ARC motif. Verify the rule against a second independent arrangement whenever available.
- Do not treat an unsuccessful guess as a validated procedure. Record uncertainty and gather discriminating evidence before spending a submission.
- When examples contain an object that could be either a stencil or an ordinary instance, test whether its non-background cells encode the same rule as the scattered elements; do not infer replication solely from proximity.

## Recoloring by repeated silhouettes (candidate rule; verify exact deltas)

When a grid contains a large line/corner-like component plus several scattered colored components, and demonstrations recolor exactly one component, test whether the recolored component's silhouette is congruent (translation, rotation, or reflection) to a component of another color. Enumerate 4-connected components, normalize their occupied-cell coordinates to their bounding-box origin, and compare exact sets under the 8 square symmetries. Use input/output cell diffs to identify the target component and the replacement color; in several examples the target matched a differently colored component while being recolored to the color of a prominent structural marker. Treat this as a candidate rule, not a guarantee.

Do not assume that any matching component is the target: demonstrations can contain repeated singleton or repeated-shape distractors, and some cases may select only one based on its relation to the prominent line/frame. If multiple congruent candidates exist, use another demo to resolve the selection predicate. If no whole-component match exists, do not improvise by recoloring the closest-looking component or a matching subpattern; investigate partial matching, connectivity convention, or a different rule. After an incorrect submission, re-derive the exact changed cells from all demos and request a discriminating example rather than cycling through nearby guesses. Preserve all non-target cells.

## Stream-task response discipline

In benchmark conversations that require an action object, the final line must contain exactly one valid action object and no additional action. Use the task's given grid dimensions and integer palette exactly. If asking for a demo, do not also submit a grid in that turn. If the instance is not over, do not use a finish action unless the protocol permits it.

## Left-anchored partial-row tail recoloring (validated task-0667a4e0)

A horizontal row may contain a solid run of one non-background color anchored at the left edge, followed by a contiguous background-color suffix. Recolor that suffix to color 1, preserving the left run and all other rows. A demonstrated 27×16 case changed row 5 (0-indexed): eight leading 4s stayed, and the eight following 0s became 1s; a separate full-width row of 4s stayed unchanged because it had no background suffix. In one solved test, row 12 had eleven leading 2s followed by five 7s; only the five-cell suffix became 1, while a full row of 2s stayed unchanged. A fresh 22×25 recurrence confirmed the same selection: row 16 had twenty leading 9s followed by five 0s, and only those five trailing 0s became 1; a separate full-width row of 9s stayed unchanged. These cases support selecting the incomplete left-anchored uniform row and changing its right suffix, independent of the leading marker and background colors. Preserve dimensions and every unrelated cell. Use a demo if a future variant has multiple partial rows, internal interruptions, or ambiguous candidate rows; do not generalize this evidence to materially different structures without checking.

**Caution for task-0667a4e0 recurrence:** Later instances under this task id differed substantially. One 12×27 case had repeated 2-row color-5 patterns in a color-8 field and eight demos; repeated suffix-to-1 hypotheses failed in all eight attempts. Some demos did show row-tail recoloring after a long full-color run, but many superficially similar tails were unchanged, so a generic last-marker/right-tail rule was not established. Treat the task ID as potentially multiple variants; do not reuse either the simple left-prefix rule or the failing broad tail guesses without exact demo-delta validation. After a failed submission, materially revise the selector and compare candidate changes against unchanged near-matches. In the 12×27 failure, rows were 2-row motifs with sparse 5 markers and alternating 5/8 segments; despite the apparent repeating patterns, no inferred continuation was validated. Preserve this as an unresolved caution, not a solution.

## Fixed-orientation L-triomino stencil in a noisy field (validated instance)

A sparse color-7 L triomino with occupied offsets `[(0,1),(1,0),(1,1)]` can serve as a stencil over scattered color-0 cells in a mostly color-9 field. In the solved instance, every translated occurrence of those exact three offsets where all three cells were 0 was recolored to 7, and all other cells—including additional 0s connected to the matches—were preserved. The marker's orientation mattered: search only the same orientation unless demonstrations establish rotations/reflections. Apply matches cellwise, allowing overlaps; do not recolor an entire connected component or all zeros in a matching component. Verify by enumerating each candidate origin and its three cells against the input before overlaying the color. This is evidence from one solved instance; confirm the predicate with demos if future instances differ in marker shape, color roles, or output behavior.

## Four-quadrant rotational tiling (validated task-dbd9720f)
When the input grid is square, task-dbd9720f transforms it into a 2H×2W canvas of four rotational copies: upper-left is the original input, upper-right is a 90° clockwise rotation, lower-left is a 90° counterclockwise rotation, and lower-right is a 180° rotation. Preserve every cell/color. Construct by block concatenation: `[[G, rotate_cw(G)], [rotate_ccw(G), rotate_180(G)]]`. This rule was supported by three demos (15×15, 13×13, 5×5), a correct 13×13 test submission, and a correct 4×4 test submission; the latter produced an 8×8 output. Thus, the concatenated result is 2H×2W. For non-square inputs, verify output dimensions/orientation from demos before assuming the same arrangement.

### Continual recurrence: task-dbd9720f
The four-rotation tiling rule also solved a fresh 11×11 test with zero wrong attempts, producing a 22×22 output. This provides independent recurrence evidence that the arrangement is UL=original, UR=90° clockwise, LL=90° counterclockwise, LR=180° rotation, by concatenating the rotated grids as blocks. Compute rotations mechanically and validate 2H×2W dimensions before submission.

A fresh 8×8 recurrence was also submitted correctly with zero wrong attempts; the expected output was 16×16. This further supports applying the four-rotation block rule to small square inputs, including asymmetric/noisy grids with no apparent panel markers. Mechanically construct all three rotations and concatenate the four blocks; verify output is 2H×2W and preserve each original cell exactly once per rotated copy. An additional independent 8×8 recurrence containing scattered colors 1, 2, 3, and 9 in a 7 field was also solved by this exact 16×16 construction, again with zero wrong submissions. A completely uniform 11×11 grid (all color 5) also yielded a correct 22×22 all-5 output under the same rule; uniformity does not change the doubled-canvas output size or require a special case.

## Cross-divider panel replication (validated)

When full horizontal and vertical divider lines partition a grid into equal panels, test whether one panel is a source tile repeated into the others. In a validated four-panel case, the lower-right panel was copied exactly to all four by translation, including background cells, with dividers unchanged. A further confirmed task-47b0cad2 case had two full color-6 horizontal dividers and one full color-6 vertical divider, producing a 3×2 array of equal 3×6 panels. The top-left panel's complete 3×6 contents (including color-1 background) were copied into all six panels at identical local offsets; preserve divider rows/column. Infer boundaries and panel sizes first, then check alignment. Treat source-panel selection and whether to copy only occupied cells or the full tile as hypotheses unless demos support them.

For a step-by-step comparison checklist and coordinate ledger, see [references/demo-analysis.md](references/demo-analysis.md).

# Ambiguous boundary rails and sparse markers: after-action caution

This Continual-ARC instance had a mostly uniform field, two separated boundary rails, and isolated marker cells (in its examples, colors and orientation varied). The examples suggested boundary-directed extensions or framed spans, but the demos were not converted into a complete coordinate-by-coordinate rule, and multiple incompatible output hypotheses remained. Several guesses (fill toward/away from a border, fill whole interiors, project marker rows, and connect frame edges) were submitted without first demonstrating exact replay across examples; all failed. This is not a solved transformation recipe.

## Reusable lesson

- Treat boundary rails plus sparse points as an ambiguous geometry class, not proof of a particular rectangle, ray, stripe, or recoloring operation.
- Build a compact delta ledger for every demo: changed coordinates and values, unchanged candidate spans, preserved rail segments, and marker behavior. Normalize coordinates to the same orientation only after checking whether demos rotate/reflect the arrangement.
- Candidate rule must predict all changed and unchanged cells in each demo. If eight examples still do not support a unique rule, do not keep making cosmetic output variants; use the remaining actions only if a new example could discriminate named hypotheses, then submit the least destructive evidence-backed result.
- Do not use demos merely because the cap permits them: analyze each received pair before requesting another. Do not use submissions as hypothesis probes when the protocol offers a demo action.

This note documents a failure mode and an analysis discipline, not a validated solve rule.

# Border-anchored stripe propagation: evidence and caution

This instance's two demonstration pairs suggest a transformation on a uniform field with long border-connected marker runs and a separate seed color.

## Exact evidence

- Demo 1: 6×5, background 1, border marker 2, interior seed 5. In rows 2–3 (1-indexed), input markers occupy column 1 and seed occupies column 3. Output converts column 1 to color 5, changes column 2 to color 5, and changes the seed at column 3 to color 4. Other cells stay put. In rows 5–6, marker 2 occupies column 5; output fills columns 1–4 with color 5, leaving the marker at column 5.
- Demo 2: 9×18, background 2, marker 8, seed 7. A marker run at the right edge occupies rows 1–3; output extends color 7 across rows 2–3 from column 2 through column 17, while row 1 remains unchanged. A marker run at the left edge occupies rows 7–9; output fills color 7 from columns 2 through 13 in rows 8–9 and recolors seed column 14 to 4. Row 7 remains unchanged.

## Candidate extrapolation

Rows in the interior of an edge-connected vertical marker segment appear to be filled horizontally toward an interior seed, with the seed changed to 4. Boundary/end-cap rows remain unchanged in demo 2. In demo 1, the marker is retained as a color-5 endpoint for rows 5–6, but the other pair changes it to 5 and uses a color-4 seed endpoint. These cases imply a directional/role-dependent rule beyond simple “fill every row between extrema”; do not generalize the candidate without identifying the seed direction and row-group exception.

## Pitfall

Avoid automatically filling all rows with an edge marker or treating both edges symmetrically. Compare exact input/output deltas, distinguishing cap rows, interior rows, which side has the marker, and whether the seed itself is overwritten. The two demos do not fully determine all mixed configurations; request another demo if a materially different arrangement is present and the score budget allows.

# Continual-ARC response protocol and recovery

## Strict response format
For an instance requiring a JSON action on every turn, respond with exactly one action object and no explanation, status text, markdown fence, or extra action. Keep the action on the final line. Avoid unrelated tool calls, repetitive TODO bookkeeping, and narration that delays the required choice.

## Demo and submission budget
A demo request has a direct score cost. Request one only when a named unresolved distinction can change the candidate output. After each demo, diff input/output exactly before deciding whether to request another. Track changed cells and informative unchanged candidate regions. Do not spend demos without incorporating earlier evidence.

## Recovery after a wrong submission
A binary incorrect signal means at least one assumption is wrong but does not reveal which. Materially revise the hypothesis, not merely its threshold or cosmetic form. Maintain a concise ledger of: transformed cells, preserved alternatives, marker color, background, geometry, endpoints, orientation, and selector. Replay every candidate rule against every demo; reject if it misses any observed change or predicts a change in an unchanged cell. In particular, sparse aligned markers alone do not validate a global bounding-box perimeter or filling every collinear interval. Use these as hypotheses only and require exact demo support.

## Candidate validation
Preserve dimensions and unchanged cells. Construct the candidate systematically; verify every row width, palette, and changed coordinate against the rule before submitting. If ambiguity persists, make the next action based on the highest-value evidence or best-supported hypothesis, and do not repeat a failed grid.

# Continual ARC: serialization checks and precedent discipline

## Grid validity before semantics
A candidate can be rejected as “not a valid ARC grid” before its transformation is evaluated. Treat that feedback separately from ordinary incorrectness. Before submission, validate that the output is a list of rows, has the intended height, every row has the intended width, and every cell is an integer in 0–9. When constructing programmatically, assert dimensions and palette before serializing. Manual copying of long grids is prone to dropped or extra cells; prefer generated rows and inspect the emitted JSON.

## Current demos outrank task-ID precedent
A recurring task ID or a stored narrow rule is only a prior. Rebuild the rule from the present instance's examples, especially when the grid structure differs. Record changed and unchanged cells per demo, distinguish candidate predicates (e.g. suffix after the last marker versus pattern continuation), and replay each candidate against the observed pairs. Do not submit a familiar rule that fails to explain even one demo or use binary rejection to justify unsupported nearby variants.

## Recovery after repeated rejection
After an invalid-grid rejection, validate structure first. After semantic incorrectness, revisit the selector, boundary, direction, replacement color, and overwrite policy as separate assumptions. If all demo requests are exhausted, make one materially evidence-based choice; do not repeat essentially the same candidate under small cosmetic variations.

# Continual ARC: evidence before extrapolation and output validation

## Why this matters
A tempting transformation can match the visible portion of one demo while still overfilling the test grid. A malformed serialized grid can also consume a submission without testing the intended hypothesis. Treat rule validation and serialization validation as separate gates.

## Evidence gate after a wrong submission
1. Re-derive the demo's exact input/output delta: list every changed coordinate and value, and inspect unchanged cells that a broad hypothesis would have modified.
2. State the current rule as a deterministic predicate, including object/marker selection, direction, gap length, endpoints, and replacement color.
3. Replay that predicate on the complete demo. Compare predicted changed cells to the actual delta; reject it if it predicts any extra or misses any actual changes.
4. After a wrong answer, do not submit a small variation of the same unverified span, line-fill, or component rule. Request an additional demo when competing rules remain and can be distinguished; otherwise choose only the rule actually supported by all evidence.

## Grid serialization gate
- Build from a copy of the input, then apply the rule programmatically wherever possible.
- Validate output height equals the intended height; every row has the same intended width; every cell is an integer in 0–9; and only licensed cells changed.
- For hand-composed JSON, validate the parsed object before submission. Do not infer correctness from visual formatting or count values by eye in a long grid.
- Keep the benchmark protocol strict: one action object per response, with no prose or second action.

## Caution
A successful serialization check only proves that a grid is well-formed; it does not establish that the transformation is correct. Require both gates before submitting.

# Continual ARC recovery for recurring lattice/downsampling tasks

Use this when a task has a regular divider lattice, output smaller than the input, or a task-specific skill with conflicting historical notes.

## Evidence-first procedure

1. Treat task-specific rules as hypotheses. First audit the current demos; historical success on an earlier variant does not prove the current mapping.
2. Record dimensions and divider/intersection coordinates explicitly. Build the sampled matrix with row/column indices; do not infer its shape by visual impression.
3. For each demo, test the complete output mapping cell by cell. If output is smaller, identify whether each output cell represents a source point, a 2x2 neighborhood, a tile, or some other footprint. Check all rows and columns, including homogeneous/background cases and edge windows.
4. List competing rules and a counterexample/prediction for each. A proposed default color, majority rule, uniform-window rule, or direct copy is not validated until it reproduces the entire demo output.
5. After any incorrect-only feedback, invalidate the submitted hypothesis and diagnose before submitting again. Do not tweak a few cells or dimensions without evidence. Re-derive the matrix, mapping, output dimensions, and predictions from the demos.
6. Request a demo when one concrete ambiguity remains and a new example can distinguish the candidates. State internally what distinction it should resolve, then inspect the new pair before spending another request or attempt.
7. Before submission, verify exact row count, row widths, palette, output dimensions, and every computed cell. Prefer deterministic construction and serialization over hand transcription.

## Pitfalls

- Wrong dimensions are a full-rule failure, not a formatting nit: derive output dimensions from multiple examples before submitting.
- A task skill may contain stale, contradictory, or demo-specific claims. Explicitly mark uncertainty and follow current evidence.
- Multiple near-identical guesses after wrong feedback waste the attempt budget. A changed default or omitted column is not a materially updated rule unless demos support it.
- Demo requests also cost points; request only when their expected information can affect the next action.

This procedure is a recovery aid, not a claim that any one lattice transform is universal.

# Continual ARC stream decision discipline

## Why this matters

A successful ARC hypothesis is only useful if the instance can be completed within its per-turn response budget. Long exploratory turns, repeated no-op tool calls, and outputs that omit the required action can consume time without improving accuracy.

## Efficient evidence cycle

1. **Read the protocol.** Track legal actions, attempt cap, demo cap, cost of demos/wrong submissions, and action-only formatting requirements.
2. **Inventory objects once.** Record dimensions, colors, connected components, bounding boxes, and shapes. Use a compact script for component summaries if the grid is large.
3. **Maintain a hypothesis ledger.** For each candidate, state the predicted changed cells and the existing evidence for/against it. Distinguish the selected object, selection condition, operation, and output color.
4. **Spend demos deliberately.** Before asking, state internally which plausible rules remain and what specific observation would separate them. A demo is worthwhile only if its result could alter the next submission.
5. **Compare deltas exactly.** After each demo, enumerate every changed coordinate/value and every salient unchanged candidate. Reject any rule that adds changes not shown or misses changes that are shown.
6. **Recover from incorrect submissions.** The binary feedback does not identify the failed assumption. Revisit object identity, selection predicate, shape equivalence (including rotations/reflections), anchors, overwrite behavior, and output value; do not submit a near-neighbor tweak without new evidence.
7. **Use tools economically.** Batch deterministic parsing, component extraction, and candidate comparison in one script. Avoid no-op commands, repetitive narrative, and multiple tool calls that do not add evidence.
8. **Act promptly.** When examples no longer distinguish remaining hypotheses, or turn time is limited, make one deliberate best-supported choice. For action-only protocols, return exactly one valid action object and no explanation; ensure it is emitted before any deadline.

## Pitfalls

- A demo request is not free; do not use it merely because uncertainty exists. It must answer a named question.
- A correct-looking transformation on the test grid is not enough: replay the candidate rule on every demo and compare the entire delta.
- If several components share a shape, verify why a particular instance is selected. Shape congruence alone may not determine the changed object; position or relationship to another motif can matter.
- Do not let open-ended reasoning delay the required protocol action or produce an empty/invalid final response.

Use alongside the core workflow and `references/incorrect-submission-recovery.md`.

# Cross-demo role normalization when palettes and dimensions vary

This class of ARC task may present demonstrations with very different grid sizes, palettes, orientations, and shapes even though the underlying operation is consistent. Avoid matching literal colors or copying coordinates from a single example. Assign semantic roles independently in each demo (e.g. boundary bars, interior markers, field, newly extended region, marker highlight), normalize geometry relative to those roles, and compare input/output deltas in role-relative coordinates.

Keep the transformation's three parts separate: (1) which object/region is selected, (2) what geometry is added, filled, or extended, and (3) how colors map. A marker recolored to a highlight color does not establish which nearby cells should be filled. Record both changed cells and plausible unchanged counterexamples, and reject hypotheses that predict extra changes.

After an incorrect submission, revisit these assumptions independently instead of making a cosmetic variant. Before spending a further demo, state at least two candidate rules and what exact observation would distinguish them. If the existing demos already vary orientation and layout, first normalize and compare those; request more examples only if a concrete ambiguity remains. In action-only stream turns, skip tool calls that do not compute or validate a stated hypothesis.

# Maintaining a delta ledger after incorrect ARC submissions

Use this when a submission receives only a binary incorrect signal. The feedback identifies no particular faulty assumption, so avoid guessing a nearby variation.

## Procedure

1. For every demonstration, compare input and output cell by cell and record every changed coordinate as `(row, column): old → new`, using one indexing convention consistently.
2. Group changed coordinates by connected component and note which original object each belongs to. Also record nearby unchanged cells that rule out overbroad fills or recolors.
3. Keep three questions separate: **selection** (why this object?), **operation** (what happens to it?), and **output value** (which color or pattern is applied?). A transformation hypothesis is incomplete if it explains the edit but not which instance is selected.
4. Replay each candidate against every demo. Reject it if it misses a changed cell or predicts any extra change. Do not submit a no-op or visually plausible fallback unless the demonstrations support it.
5. Request another demo only when you can name the competing hypotheses and describe what arrangement would distinguish them. Otherwise use the available examples to resolve the hypotheses before spending another action.
6. Only submit after the complete candidate matches every demonstrated delta; validate dimensions, row lengths, palette, and preservation of unrelated cells.

Binary correctness feedback cannot diagnose a failed assumption. Keep the ledger across actions and explicitly revisit object selection, geometry, orientation, anchor, overwrite behavior, and target/output color before the next attempt.

This supplements `references/incorrect-submission-recovery.md` and `references/demo-analysis.md` in the ARC reasoning umbrella.

# Demo comparison and hypothesis ledger

Use one ledger row per observation/example and write coordinates consistently (0-indexed or 1-indexed, never mixed).

## Comparison checklist

- Record input/output dimensions and background color.
- List non-background objects/components with color, bounding box, cell coordinates, and shape.
- For each input object or marker, inspect its exact output neighborhood. Determine whether it persists, changes color, expands, moves, or is replaced.
- Track any distinctive source motif separately from scattered objects. Test whether the motif is a rule stencil, a pre-existing example, or unrelated decoration.
- For each candidate transformation, record the predicted changed coordinates and compare against the output. Reject a hypothesis if any unexplained changed or unchanged cell remains.
- Check border cases, overlapping placements, and whether output values overwrite existing cells.

## Hypothesis ledger template

| Candidate rule | Evidence it explains | Prediction that distinguishes it | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
|  |  |  |  |

Before requesting a demo, name the ambiguity and the observation that would discriminate candidates. After receiving it, update the ledger before choosing another demo or submitting.

## Candidate-grid validation

1. Generate from a copy of the input, not a blank grid, unless examples show full reconstruction.
2. Apply only cells warranted by the rule; preserve unrelated cells.
3. Verify dimensions, row lengths, palette, and each placement at the intended anchor/orientation.
4. Check that a generated candidate obeys every demonstration when the same transformation is replayed on its input.
5. Inspect the complete output representation before submitting, especially boundary clipping and overlaps.

# Doubled-canvas quadrant audit

Use this audit when a demo output has dimensions 2H×2W and appears to contain four copies/variants of an H×W input.

1. Split each output into blocks `TL`, `TR`, `BL`, `BR`, each exactly H×W.
2. Compare `TL` against the original input cell-for-cell; do not assume it is unchanged based on appearance.
3. Compare other blocks to the input under identity, 90°/180°/270° rotations, reflections, transpose, and any candidate row/column ordering. For square inputs, check all eight dihedral symmetries. If the block has a different dimension than the input, account for rotation swapping H and W.
4. Check every demo, including small examples. Histograms and visual resemblance are useful filters but are not a full match.
5. Once a rule fits all demos, build the output by block concatenation, then verify its full dimensions, row widths, and each quadrant.

In task-dbd9720f, all three demonstrations supported the exact layout `[[G, rotate_cw(G)], [rotate_ccw(G), rotate_180(G)]]` for square input G. The test was 10×10, so the submitted output was a 20×20 grid. This is a solved instance example, not a universal rule for doubled canvases.

# Evidence ledger after an incorrect submission

This is a supporting checklist for ARC stream tasks with several colors and many disconnected components, especially when only one or a few objects change.

## Before requesting another demo

1. Enumerate exact input/output deltas for every available pair: coordinates, input value, output value, and connected component.
2. Record unchanged components that look like candidate matches; these are negative evidence against broad selection rules.
3. Separate three questions: which object is selected, what operation is applied, and how its output color/value is chosen.
4. Write at least two live hypotheses and the specific observation in another demo that would distinguish them. Request only if that observation could alter the answer; demo requests consume budget.

## Before another submission

1. Treat incorrect feedback as confirmation that the whole candidate is wrong, not as a diagnosis of which assumption failed.
2. Revisit selection, transformation, color mapping, orientation/anchor, and overwrite behavior independently.
3. Require one rule to replay exactly on every demo, including the unchanged counterexamples. Do not resubmit the same grid or a cosmetic variant without evidence changing a named assumption.
4. Build the output as a copy of the test input, change only licensed cells, and validate dimensions and every modified coordinate.

Avoid replacing exact comparison with visual resemblance or speculative narratives. Do not spend tool calls on actions that neither calculate the delta nor test a stated hypothesis.

# Gapped marker rows and suffix recoloring

## Pattern and exact delta
Three demonstrations show a uniform field with a marker-color horizontal row beginning at the left edge. In each transformed row, cells strictly to the right of the rightmost marker are recolored to color 1. The marker cells and all cells through the rightmost marker are preserved. Rows not beginning with the marker pattern are not transformed. A row with a full-width marker has no suffix.

One test case extended this rule to internal gaps and separated islands: a row began with marker color 7, included gaps and a non-marker cell before later marker cells, then had another marker island near the right edge. The supported extrapolation is to find the rightmost 7 in that qualifying row and recolor only the strict suffix after it to 1. Do not fill the internal gaps or recolor intervening non-marker cells. Other rows that contain marker color but do not start with it remain unchanged.

## Evidence limits and workflow

The demos established the suffix operation and row qualification, but did not themselves include the same gapped/multi-island structure as the test. Treat the rightmost-marker extension as the simplest consistent rule, not as directly demonstrated. If demo budget allows and a competing contiguous-run rule would change the answer, request a discriminating demo. Otherwise preserve all cells through the rightmost marker and alter only the suffix. Validate the complete row-by-row delta and exact output color before submission.

# Recovering after an incorrect ARC submission

An incorrect/incorrect-only signal confirms that the full candidate is wrong, but does not identify the failed assumption. Avoid spending subsequent attempts on near-neighbor variants of the same guessed transformation.

## Recovery sequence

1. Compare each demonstration input and output cell-by-cell; record the exact changed coordinates and unchanged counterexamples.
2. Replay the candidate rule on the demonstration input. Reject it if it predicts any changed cell incorrectly or predicts changes where the demo preserves cells.
3. Write down the assumptions separately: which object is transformed, target color, geometry, direction, anchor, endpoint inclusion, overwrite semantics, and whether the change is local or global.
4. Use an available demo request when a concrete competing hypothesis remains and a new example can distinguish it. State what observation would separate the candidates before requesting.
5. Only resubmit after new evidence or a materially improved rule. Validate the complete grid (dimensions, every row, palette, changed coordinates) against all examples.

## Sparse-marker caution

A set of collinear or row/column-aligned markers invites plausible span, enclosure, or completion rules. Do not infer which cells should change from visual appeal alone. A single example may fail to distinguish connecting markers from completing a larger shape or applying another geometric relation. Require the exact demonstrated delta to support the rule; if it does not, request another arrangement instead of guessing a modified fill.

# Lattice-crossing window decoding: evidence and safeguards

## Demonstrated variant

A 29×26 grid used a repeated field color 1, horizontal separator rows of color 2 every 3 rows, and vertical separator columns of color 2 every 4 columns. Sparse non-2 colors were written at some separator crossings. Sampling the crossings at rows `1,4,7,...,28` and columns `3,7,11,15,19,23` produced a 10×6 marker matrix.

The output was generated from the smallest rectangular crop containing all non-background crossing markers (here matrix rows 4–9 and columns 0–3, a 6×4 crop). Scan overlapping 2×2 windows within that crop: emit the common marker color when all four entries are equal; otherwise emit the original field color 1. This yields a 5×3 output and exactly matches the demonstrated output:

`[[1,9,1],[9,9,1],[1,1,1],[1,1,4],[8,1,4]]`.

The crop choice matters: reducing the whole crossing matrix or using a non-overlapping block transform gives the wrong size/alignment. Derive the crossing coordinates from the repeated separator spacing, and locate the active marker crop from the data rather than assuming the entire lattice is the encoded image.

## Safeguards

- Treat this as a demonstrated variant, not a universal lattice rule. Another example in the same task family had a different apparent crossing matrix/output correspondence, so do not apply this transform unless it reproduces every available demo exactly.
- Identify the field/background color from the repeated interior cells; it is the fallback output for mixed 2×2 windows in this variant, not the separator color.
- Validate crop bounds, output dimensions (`crop_height - 1` by `crop_width - 1`), and every window against the demo outputs before using the rule on a test.
- After an incorrect submission, revisit separator coordinates and crop bounds before changing colors or inventing another default. A wrong output can arise from the wrong active crop even if the local window rule is right.
- Keep coordinates zero-based in scripts and explicitly list the sampled rows/columns to avoid off-by-one errors.

# Inferring selective recoloring across many components

Use this checklist when a demo grid has many disconnected objects and only a subset is recolored.

1. Extract the exact input/output delta: coordinates, source color, destination color, and component identity. Record unchanged components as negative evidence.
2. Describe each changed component using shape occupancy, size, orientation, bounds, position, adjacency, and relations to other components. Keep target selection separate from destination-color selection.
3. Test candidate selection predicates and color mappings against every demo, including unchanged counterexamples. A plausible visual resemblance is insufficient if it would select other preserved components.
4. Determine whether the output color is fixed, supplied by a marker, or varies with another feature; verify against multiple examples before applying it.
5. On the test, modify only cells licensed by the validated selector and mapping. Preserve all other cells.
6. If hypotheses remain, request a demo only when their predicted changed-cell sets differ. After an incorrect submission, revisit selector, mapping, and component identity rather than making a cosmetic variant.

Common trap: a visually prominent color suggests the destination, so the solver recolors a large-looking component while skipping the harder question of why that component—and not the many unchanged objects—was selected. Exact deltas and negative examples should constrain the rule.

# Noisy rectangular object cleanup: inference checklist

This reference records a hypothesis to test when demonstrations contain solid rectangular color regions, apparent holes or intrusions, and scattered pixels.

## Establish the transformation from demos

1. Compare input and output cell-by-cell. List changed cells and their original/new colors.
2. Group changed cells by connected region and compare them with candidate object bounding boxes.
3. Check whether interior interruptions are replaced by the object's color, whether external speckles disappear, and whether any boundary cells change.
4. Verify the same operation across every object and demo. Do not infer that all external non-background cells are noise unless outputs support that.

## Apply only when supported

Record exact half-open or inclusive row/column bounds for each object. Create the candidate from the input, fill or clean only the cells the demos license, and preserve every other cell. Validate rows/columns at object boundaries and compare the complete generated grid against the source. Scripted output construction is useful for transcription but does not validate the inferred rule.

## Pitfall

A visually plausible rectangle-cleanup explanation is not enough: if the demonstration shows only one example, distinguish whole-bounding-box fill from removal of isolated noise and from selective recoloring. A mistaken edge bound or treating an object as noise can cause a wrong submission. If unresolved and demos are available, request a discriminating example before spending a submission.

# Global palette remapping with preserved geometry

When demonstrations preserve cell locations and shapes but recolor every cell by its original color, test a global palette substitution before inferring a geometric transformation. Compare corresponding cells and write the mapping explicitly as `input value -> output value`; verify each source color maps consistently and that no cells move, appear, or disappear. Transfer semantic color roles—not numeric values—to fresh instances.

Before submission, validate the mapping on one known background cell and one marker cell, confirm the output palette and dimensions, and inspect a representative row. Common pitfalls include reversing source and target roles or using an incorrect replacement literal in code. Treat this as a candidate only when the full demo delta supports it.

# Panel overlay and marker-filter analysis

Use this checklist for ARC grids divided into aligned panels by a solid separator, especially when one panel contains sparse markers and the other a dense pattern.

## Reliable inference procedure

1. Record exact dimensions and locate separator rows/columns. Extract each panel independently, excluding separators, and verify their dimensions and alignment.
2. Classify each panel's colors and roles from structure, not color frequency. For a sparse-marker panel, list every marker coordinate. For the patterned panel, define explicit candidate predicates such as `cell == X`, `cell != background`, or membership in a motif.
3. Build a coordinate-by-coordinate truth table for all markers in each demonstration. Compare the output at aligned coordinates to candidate relations: marker AND pattern foreground, marker AND pattern background, marker OR pattern, equality, and color-specific conditions. Include negative cases—markers where the second panel has each possible value—not only output positives.
4. Infer the exact output dimensions, background value, and selected-cell value separately. A panel can contribute a predicate without contributing its colors to the output. Do not automatically preserve a panel's source cells in the result.
5. Replay the inferred operation on the whole demonstration and require exact equality with the supplied output. Any unexplained output cell or missing expected cell invalidates the rule.
6. Apply the identical panel-relative coordinate mapping to the test instance. Construct the full output and validate every cell, dimensions, palette, and preservation/removal behavior before submitting.

## Common failure modes

- Matching a marker to the wrong panel color because the dense color is mistaken for the background, or vice versa.
- Assuming the output is a recoloring of the entire marker panel when only an intersection or filter is retained.
- Using row/column spans, motif copying, or the visually salient top panel before testing simple cellwise Boolean filtering.
- Checking only positive output coordinates; negatives among markers are what distinguish foreground intersection from other hypotheses.
- Generating an answer without replaying the candidate rule exactly on the demonstration.

## This session's diagnostic pattern

A demo showed a grid separated by a solid vertical line into a sparse marker panel and a dense binary-pattern panel, with a lower-dimension output containing only selected marker cells recolored. The important general lesson is to test the aligned coordinate-wise intersection between sparse markers and the pattern's visually distinct foreground, and to establish foreground/background from explicit output positives and negatives rather than frequency or intuition. This is a hypothesis to verify against all demo coordinates, not a universal ARC rule.

# Repeated-silhouette recoloring: evidence and recovery

Treat silhouette matching as a hypothesis, not a complete rule. In complicated ARC recoloring puzzles, target selection and replacement-color choice can be independent; demos under this task family have shown that recoloring a visually congruent component to the prominent marker color can fail even when an older instance fit that pattern.

## Evidence ledger per demo

For every input/output pair, record the exact changed coordinates, the connected component containing them, its before/after colors, all congruent components under translation/rotation/reflection, and unchanged congruent components as negative evidence. Test candidate selection predicates and color-transfer mappings across all demos. A prominent line, sparse marker, or matching component is not by itself proof of its role.

## After incorrect submissions

An incorrect response only rejects the entire candidate; it does not reveal which component or rule element was wrong. Do not resubmit the same grid or cosmetic variants. Revisit selector, operation, output color, connectivity/orientation, and overwrite semantics separately. Request a demo only if it distinguishes concrete live hypotheses and could change the next candidate. Keep changes limited to cells licensed by a rule that explains every demo.

## Continual-ARC interaction discipline

Return exactly one valid action JSON object per turn, with no surrounding explanation. Avoid repeated exploratory turns and needless demo requests: after each example extract exact deltas before requesting another, and submit promptly once evidence supports a rule. Preserve the grid dimensions and all unaffected cells.

# Selective marker-span extensions

This reference captures a recurring ARC pattern where a third color is added to portions of a sparse, mostly rectilinear marker pattern. It is specifically a caution against assuming that all row/column spans between markers should be filled.

## Reliable inference procedure

1. For each demo, record the exact coordinates that changed and their output values. Treat the added color separately from the original marker color.
2. Identify each original straight run and candidate gaps. Distinguish unit gaps, longer gaps, endpoints, intersections, and overlapping horizontal/vertical candidates.
3. Test simple predicates (for example: any two markers in a row/column, only consecutive markers with a one-cell gap, paired side segments, or boundary outline completion) against every demo. A candidate must predict the *entire* changed-cell set, not merely a subset.
4. Check that existing marker cells remain unchanged and that all unrelated background cells remain intact. Some tasks add the third color only to selected missing positions and do not complete the outline or connect every pair of collinear markers.
5. After each incorrect submission, explicitly identify what the failed candidate predicted that was not licensed by examples. Do not resubmit a minor variation of the same broad span hypothesis without new evidence.
6. Request a demo only for a named ambiguity and a concrete expected discriminator. Track the demo cap and submission budget; when demonstrations are exhausted, apply the best-supported rule without claiming certainty.

## Pitfalls

- Filling between every pair of same-color extrema overproduces cells in tasks that select only certain gaps.
- Filling a rectangle perimeter based on global bounds can be equally unsupported.
- Even a unit-gap rule should be verified: added cells may depend on local structure beyond opposite markers.
- The grid's dominant color and visually apparent shape are not sufficient evidence; compare exact cells across examples.

Use this checklist alongside the core ARC hypothesis-validation workflow in `SKILL.md`.

# Selective frame and collinear-gap caution

This task-b0680534 instance was not solved. Multiple submissions applying the global marker bounding-box perimeter, all row/column spans, and combinations of those rules were rejected. The demonstrations show that additions can occur on outer edges and in internal aligned gaps, while other plausible perimeter/spans remain unchanged; even a closed rectangular outline can be left as-is. Thus neither global-bounds completion nor blanket collinear interpolation is a validated rule.

## Reusable workflow

1. For every demo, diff input/output and record every added cell plus nearby candidate gaps that stayed background. Use consistent zero-based coordinates.
2. Separate candidate groups (outer border, interior row gaps, interior column gaps) and enumerate their lengths, endpoints, neighboring marker patterns, and neighboring frame geometry.
3. Form explicit selectors that explain both positive and negative examples. Replay each selector on all demos; reject on even one false positive or missed addition.
4. A task-specific precedent may help enumerate hypotheses, but is not evidence that today's arrangement follows the same predicate. A wrong submission only tells you that a candidate was incomplete; it does not justify changing one arbitrary threshold.
5. When the selector is still unknown, spend demos only on a stated ambiguity. After demo cap, choose only a materially evidence-backed hypothesis; don't repeat cosmetic versions of a disproven broad rule.

## Observation from the failed instance

Eight demos were available. Their demonstrated outputs were selective rather than a consistent global bounding frame or all-extrema row/column fill. The attempted global perimeter and blanket spans did not predict all unchanged/changed cells, and the held-out output remained unknown after repeated incorrect submissions. No specific replacement selector is established here; do not treat this note as an answer recipe.

# Transfer the selection rule, not just the color

A demo that changes every cell in a complete uniform row from one color to another does not establish a global palette substitution. The unchanged uniform rows are counterexamples: the recoloring is conditional on a structural selector. Keep the hypothesis split into (1) selection predicate, (2) selected unit (cell, row, component, etc.), and (3) color operation. Replay the candidate on the demo and ensure it predicts every changed and unchanged cell.

When the test has a different structure from the demo (for example, diagonal fragments rather than full-width stripes), do not generalize by recoloring a visually prominent object or by mapping all occurrences of the changed input color. Request a demo that presents the relevant structure or otherwise discriminates the candidate selectors. Following an incorrect broad recoloring, reopen both the selector and operation; incorrect-only feedback does not tell which assumption failed.

Continual ARC workflow: note demo caps and attempt costs, but spend a demo when the only demonstration supports multiple rules with divergent test predictions. Emit exactly one protocol action per turn; avoid unsupported retries based on the same evidence.
